passage: Coordinator's note, community centre. I'm Yamini, and I'm writing down what I saw Kalyani do, because it was quicker than most of us manage. Kalyani had drafted a one-page guide for new volunteers. It was good but not polished: one paragraph was clumsy, and the map was hand-drawn. Instead of holding it for another week, Kalyani printed five copies and gave them to two volunteers, the caretaker and me with a line at the top: “Version one. Tell me what's wrong.” Within two days we had eleven comments, mostly about the map and the opening hours. Kalyani fixed those and posted version two on the noticeboard on Friday. I would have waited a month.

qa.q: How many copies did Kalyani print for the first round?
qa.a: Kalyani printed five copies for the first round.

qa.q: What did Kalyani feel about handing over an unpolished guide?
qa.a: Kalyani seems comfortable and practical rather than anxious, treating the rough version as a way to learn what needs fixing.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do after receiving eleven comments?
qa.a: Kalyani fixed the map and opening hours and posted version two on the noticeboard on Friday.

qa.q: How does Yamini see Kalyani's approach compared with Yamini's own?
qa.a: Yamini is impressed and slightly humbled, admitting that Yamini would have waited a month for a perfect version.

grounding: A worker ships a good-enough version, gathers feedback and improves it instead of waiting for perfection.

passage: Saturday. Today I sent Ramesh the first draft of the housing society newsletter, eight pages, at about sixty percent: two photos missing, the back page empty. Every instinct said wait a week, make it perfect. Instead I typed, “Rough draft. Please tell me where I'm going wrong,” and pressed send before my nerves could vote. My stomach fizzed for an hour. Ramesh, who edited the newsletter for years, phoned that evening. “The front page is good. Move the notices to the back. You do not need eight pages.” Two comments, and I had the shape of the whole thing. I wouldn't have found that alone in a month. Tomorrow I cut it to six. — Wasim

qa.q: What did Wasim type when sending the draft to Ramesh?
qa.a: Wasim typed, “Rough draft. Please tell me where I'm going wrong,” and sent it.

qa.q: Why did Wasim's stomach fizz for an hour after sending?
qa.a: Wasim felt nervous about showing an unfinished draft, an ordinary worry after sending something imperfect.

qa.q: What did the early feedback change about Wasim's plan?
qa.a: Ramesh's two comments, to move the notices to the back and cut the pages, gave Wasim the shape of the newsletter, so Wasim would cut it to six pages.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel about receiving the rough draft?
qa.a: Ramesh, who edited the newsletter for years, probably feels respected and pleased to be asked, and can give useful advice quickly.

grounding: A mature worker ships a good-enough draft, gets feedback and improves it rather than holding it for perfection.

passage: Keerthana had started a small tailoring unit in her family's front room in Palani, stitching cloth shopping bags. For two months she had been perfecting the first batch: redoing handles, changing the fabric, re-cutting pockets. Her cousin Shreya, who ran a provision store, finally said, "Give me twenty. Whatever state they're in. Let customers decide." Keerthana's stomach turned. Two bags had slightly uneven seams. She delivered all twenty anyway, with a notebook for comments. In a week, fourteen had sold. Customers wrote that they wanted a longer strap and a zip. Nobody wrote about the seams. Keerthana bought zips on Monday and started the second batch, lighter than she'd felt in months.

qa.q: How many bags did Keerthana deliver to Shreya?
qa.a: She delivered all twenty.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she handed over bags with uneven seams?
qa.a: Her stomach turned; she felt nervous and exposed, worried the imperfect seams would be judged.

qa.q: What did the good-enough batch teach Keerthana that months of perfecting did not?
qa.a: Real customers wanted a longer strap and a zip, feedback she only got by letting the imperfect bags leave the room.

qa.q: How does Shreya see the two months of perfecting?
qa.a: Shreya seems to see it as holding back for no reason, and pushes her cousin to let customers decide.

grounding: Shows a young worker releasing a good-enough first batch, getting feedback and improving instead of chasing perfection.

passage: Alejandro, in his second year teaching Spanish at a secondary school in Seville, had been building a set of grammar worksheets for weeks. He wanted every page perfect: the right pictures, no mistakes, clever examples. His colleague Astrid watched him redo page four for the third time. "Just give them to one class tomorrow," she said. "See where they get stuck." He winced, but he printed ten pages that night, typos included. The next day, a student pointed out a mistake in exercise six. Three students were confused by the instructions on page two. Alejandro rewrote those two things that evening. By Friday version two went to all his classes.

qa.q: Which exercise had a mistake in it?
qa.a: A student pointed out a mistake in exercise six.

qa.q: What was Alejandro feeling when Astrid suggested using the worksheets tomorrow?
qa.a: He winced, feeling uneasy and exposed at the thought of showing imperfect pages to students.

qa.q: Which approach worked better, and why?
qa.a: Using a good-enough version with one class quickly showed the real problems in exercise six and page two, which weeks of polishing had not found.

qa.q: How might the students be affected by version two?
qa.a: They get clearer instructions and correct exercises, shaped by the problems they themselves pointed out.

grounding: Illustrates a worker using an imperfect version, gathering feedback and improving it instead of holding out for perfection.

passage:
At the city library's community office, Eshaan had spent a week on the new reading-hour flyer for children. It was decent: the time, the place, a drawing of an owl. But he wanted better colours, a second design and maybe a Tamil version.
His colleague Karthik leaned over. "Print fifty of this one. Put them up on Monday. See what the parents say."
"It's not finished."
"It's finished enough to learn from."
Eshaan printed fifty. He put them in the children's section and at two schools nearby.
By Friday, three parents had told the desk the same thing: they couldn't tell if the reading hour was free. Eshaan hadn't thought of that. Two others asked for a Tamil version.
He added "Free, all welcome" in large letters, made the Tamil version and printed the second batch the next Monday.
Twenty-two children came to the first reading hour. Eshaan pinned the first, imperfect flyer above his desk.

qa.q: How many flyers did Eshaan print first?
qa.a: Eshaan printed fifty.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel about printing the flyer before it was perfect?
qa.a: Eshaan felt reluctant and uneasy, believing the flyer was not finished.

qa.q: What did sending out the imperfect version teach Eshaan?
qa.a: Parents' feedback showed the flyer didn't say it was free and that a Tamil version was wanted, things Eshaan hadn't thought of.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel when twenty-two children came?
qa.a: Karthik would likely feel pleased and a little vindicated that printing early worked.

grounding: Illustrates a worker who ships a good-enough flyer, gets feedback and improves it instead of holding it for perfection.
